::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Basic identity for Cayley's theorem proof](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4921385/basic-identity-for-cayleys-theorem-proof), asked by [Amanda Wealth](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1158735/amanda-wealth) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2024-05-23; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I was studying graph theory when a question came to my mind.
>
> The proof of Cayley's theorem (as in Wilson's "Introduction to graph theory", p. 69) is somehow clear, I just can't realise why the last equality holds (which should be easy since it's not explained anywhere). WolframAlpha confirms its validity as well. It's the following:
> $$\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(n-1)^{-k+n-1}\binom{n-2}{k-1} = n^{n-2}$$
> The text gives the intermediate passage $\{(n-1)+1\}^{n-2}$. Can anyone enlighten me?
>
>
>   [q-1]: iEPSIGj8.png
:::

This looks like a pretty straightforward application of the binomial theorem. For a natural number $N$, we have
$$\sum_{i=0}^N \binom{N}{i} x^{N-i}y^i = (x+y)^N$$
If we set $N=n-2$, $x=n-1$, and $y=1$, we get
$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-2} \binom{n-2}{i} (n-1)^{n-2-i} \cdot 1^i = ((n-1)+1)^{n-2} = n^{n-2}$$
Now reindex the sum by setting $k=i+1$. We get
$$n^{n-2} = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \binom{n-2}{k-1}(n-1)^{n-2-(k-1)}
    = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \binom{n-2}{k-1}(n-1)^{-k+n-1}$$
